newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Gujral calls for more regional cooperation.
newsitem.headline: India's Gujral calls for more regional cooperation.

text.p: Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujaral on Friday reiterated India's opposition to a global treaty banning nuclear tests and said the nation wanted better ties with its neighbours including arch-rival Pakistan.
Gujral stressed greater regional cooperation in his nationally televised address to the nation on its 50th anniversary of independence.

"Our foreign policy emphasises regional cooperation. We want to improve relations with neighbours, but will not make any compromises on national security," Gujral said from the 17th century Red Fort in Delhi.

On India's reluctance to sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT), he said: "We will not sign the CTBT under any pressure unless it applies equally to all and countries that have these weapons agree to destroy them."
Last year, India refused to sign the treaty, insisting that the five declared nuclear powers -- Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States -- first vow to eliminate their arsenals.

Gujral said if all of South Asia moved together, it could rival any other trading bloc. He said the fight against poverty would be successful if all seven countries in the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) moved forward together.
SAARC is composed of Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

Gujral said there had been a marked improvement in India's relations with Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal. "The time has come for Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and India's northeast region to move forward together."
He said a 30-year old insurgency in the northeastern state of Nagaland, which borders Burma, was on the wane.
Gujral said both India and Pakistan wanted to move towards friendship after 50 years of rivalry, and a third round of peace talks between senior diplomats were scheduled in New Delhi in September.

"Friendship is only possible between nations when there is no interference in each others' domestic affairs. Let us all make promises to each other that we will not interfere in each other's domestic affairs."

New Delhi accuses Pakistan of arming and training guerrillas fighting Indian rule in Jammu and Kashmir state, where police and hospitals say some 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since a separatist revolt erupted in 1990.
Pakistan says it provides only diplomatic and moral support to the guerrillas.
